clue.text: Linguistically explain speed of light, astronomical unit

parts.note: to parse a sentence is to analyse its grammar
c is the physics symbol for the speed of light

explanation.surface: A physics lecturer struggling to put the speed of light and astronomical units into words.
explanation.walkthrough: The comma makes 'astronomical unit' look like part of a list of physics terms, but it is the definition sitting at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: A parsec is a measure of interstellar distance, about 3.26 light years, used by astronomers.

clue.text: Make up very early in the day?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: make amends for a wrong
second meaning, split into two words: the time one o'clock in the morning

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests putting on make-up at dawn; the question mark warns that the second half must be read as two words, AT ONE, a time just after midnight.
explanation.definitionFit: To atone is to make amends or compensate for a wrong done, which is one sense of making up.

clue.text: Poet on electronic system accessing prophet

indicators.note: to access something is to get inside it, so one part goes into another

parts.note: a seer foresees the future
taken as written
the net is the internet

explanation.surface: A poet logging on to some electronic system to consult a prophet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On' looks like a mere preposition in the surface but supplies two letters of its own; 'electronic system' is the internet.
explanation.definitionFit: A sonneteer is a writer of sonnets, so a type of poet, often used slightingly for a minor versifier.

clue.text: Appeal having snaffled that woman's cricket ball

indicators.note: to snaffle is to grab and keep hold of, so one part takes another inside it

parts.note: a cry is an appeal or plea
possessive pronoun for a female person

explanation.surface: A fielder's appeal after a woman has pinched the cricket ball.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket slang a new, shiny red ball is the cherry. 'Appeal' looks like the cricketing howl to the umpire, which suits the surface but here just means a cry.
explanation.definitionFit: Cricket players call the ball a cherry, especially a new one, from its bright red colour and round shape.

clue.text: Vitreous matter I said, no rocks, black parts

indicators.note: to part something is to split it open, so one letter is wedged inside the rest
as a verb, to rock is to shake about, so these letters are tossed into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder
B is the abbreviation for black, as on pencils

explanation.surface: Someone insisting a glassy substance contains no rocks, just black bits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rocks' looks like the geology of the surface but is the anagram signal; the rearranged letters are then split after the first O to take B.
explanation.definitionFit: Obsidian is a natural volcanic glass, so its texture is literally vitreous, or glass-like.

clue.text: Old Oscar winner floating on air

indicators.note: in a down entry, one thing placed on another sits above it, so the first part comes before the second

parts.note: something floating is on the water
an air is a manner or show put on, as is a front

explanation.surface: An elderly Oscar winner so delighted that they are floating on air.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Floating on air' is an idiom for being elated, which hides the two separate pieces; 'air' here means an assumed manner.
explanation.definitionFit: The 1954 Marlon Brando picture won the Academy Award for Best Picture, so it is a classic film that took an Oscar.

clue.text: Dark, alert snakes captivated by sibilant sound?

indicators.note: something captivated is held captive, so it sits inside the other part

parts.note: a hiss, written as a string of esses

indicators.note: as a verb, to snake is to wind and twist, so these letters wriggle into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: Watchful snakes in the dark, charmed by a hissing noise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Snakes' sits naturally beside the hissing, but it is a verb telling you to rearrange the word before it.
explanation.definitionFit: A starless night is one with no stars visible, hence without light and so dark.

clue.text: Opening in dip, long channel

indicators.note: the opening of a word is where it begins, so only its first letter is kept

parts.note: the first letter of the word
to long for something is to itch for it

explanation.surface: A hole in a dip in the ground leading to a long water channel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Long' reads as an adjective describing the channel, but it is a verb meaning yearn.
explanation.definitionFit: A ditch is a narrow trench dug for drainage, so it serves as a channel for water.

clue.text: Identify a crime where suspicious crate's imported

indicators.note: goods imported are brought in, so these letters are carried inside the others

parts.note: a sin is a crime or wrongdoing

indicators.note: something suspicious is dodgy or not right, so these letters are out of order

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A customs officer identifying smuggling, where a dodgy crate has been brought into the country.
explanation.walkthrough: The rearranged CRATE goes into A SIN, after the S. The surface of contraband makes 'imported' look literal.
explanation.definitionFit: To ascertain is to find out for certain, which is to establish or identify a fact.

clue.text: Plant in teapot is sprawling

indicators.note: something sprawling spreads out untidily, so these letters are scattered into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A houseplant growing out of a teapot and sprawling everywhere.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like a link placing the plant in the pot, but it is part of the letters to be rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: The poinsettia is a Mexican shrub with red bracts, widely sold as a Christmas houseplant.

clue.text: Nail course of action

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a small, sharp, broad-headed nail
second meaning: an approach or line taken, as in try a different one

explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads like an instruction to nail down a plan; the two halves are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: A tack is a short pin with a flat head; from sailing, it is also a policy or direction of approach.

clue.text: Train picks up last of people after evacuation of Rome

indicators.note: following something means coming later in the line, so the rest goes behind it
evacuating a place empties it, so only the outside letters of the word remain

parts.note: the word with its middle emptied out
to pick up a sound is to hear it

indicators.note: the last of something is its final part, so only its closing letter is used

parts.note: the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: A train collecting the last passengers after Rome has been evacuated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Train' looks like the railway but is a verb, the definition; 'picks up' means hears, not collects.
explanation.definitionFit: To rehearse is to practise a performance repeatedly, so to train or drill for it.

clue.text: Asian city I understand bound by traditions

indicators.note: something bound by another is tied up and enclosed within it

parts.note: lore is the body of traditions of a people
an exclamation of comprehension

explanation.surface: A visitor to an Asian city who finds it hemmed in by its customs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I understand' is one exclamation, the sound someone makes when it clicks.
explanation.definitionFit: Lahore is the capital of Punjab province in Pakistan and one of the largest cities in South Asia.

clue.text: Somewhat sweet, we established?

indicators.note: somewhat means to some extent, so only part of the following words is used

parts.note: spans the end of the first word, the whole second and the start of the third

explanation.surface: Two people agreeing, a little unsure, that something is rather sweet.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue does double duty: read as wordplay it is a hidden word, read whole it is a tentative description of something rather sweet.
explanation.definitionFit: Twee means excessively dainty or quaint, cloyingly pretty, which is sweetness taken too far.

clue.text: Question ludicrous dope leading party in White House furore?

indicators.note: what leads goes in front, so this part comes before the next

parts.note: a question word

indicators.note: something ludicrous is absurd and topsy-turvy, so these letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder
a do is a party

explanation.surface: A ludicrous dope at the head of a party, causing uproar in the White House.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags a definition by example: a fuss in Washington is one kind of the commotion meant. 'Dope' is just letters to shuffle, not a fool.
explanation.definitionFit: Whoop-de-do is informal for noisy excitement or commotion, a hullabaloo or fuss over something.

clue.text: European chambers occupied by American nationals, primarily

indicators.note: a space occupied by someone has them inside it

parts.note: atria are chambers of the heart
US is the abbreviation for American, as in US citizen

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so just the opening letter is taken

parts.note: the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: Rooms in Europe mainly occupied by American citizens.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chambers' suggests rooms or parliaments, but the setter wants the heart's chambers, the atria. 'Primarily' applies only to the word right before it.
explanation.definitionFit: An Austrian is a native or citizen of Austria, a country in central Europe.

clue.text: Great fun scoffing meat — banger?

indicators.note: to scoff food is to wolf it down, so one part swallows another

parts.note: a riot is something hugely entertaining
flesh is the meat of an animal

explanation.surface: Having a great time wolfing down meat, with a sausage on the side.
explanation.walkthrough: A banger is British slang for a sausage, which suits the eating surface; the question mark says to read it literally instead, as something that goes bang.
explanation.definitionFit: A gunshot from a rifle makes a loud bang, so it is jokingly something that bangs.

clue.text: Titanic, casualty featured in item of mine?

indicators.note: something featured in a work appears within it, so it is placed inside

parts.note: coal is dug from a mine
a casualty is a loss, as in losses in battle

explanation.surface: The Titanic disaster, with a victim of a sea mine.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital T makes 'Titanic' look like the ship, which ties in with casualty and mines; it is the adjective meaning huge.
explanation.definitionFit: Titanic means of enormous size or strength, as does colossal, from the giant statue at Rhodes.

clue.text: Small group of us, more at sixes and sevens!

indicators.note: the idiom means in total disarray, so these letters are muddled

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A little band of friends, with more joining, all in confusion.
explanation.walkthrough: The numbers in the indicator tease the number hidden in the answer. 'At sixes and sevens' is an idiom for being in a muddle.
explanation.definitionFit: A foursome is a set of four people, as at golf or doubles tennis, which is a small party.

clue.text: Ultimately aloof superhero, Batman resident in Gotham, for example

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so each word gives up only its final letter

parts.note: the closing letters of four consecutive words

explanation.surface: A standoffish superhero, Batman, living in Gotham City.
explanation.walkthrough: Gotham looks like Batman's home city, the obvious picture; but Gotham is also a well-known typeface. 'Ultimately' applies to all four words, not only the first.
explanation.definitionFit: Gotham is a sans-serif typeface designed in 2000, used widely in signage, so it is one example of a typeface.

clue.text: Day getting close, bruv

parts.note: FRI is the short form of Friday
the close of something is its end

explanation.surface: Someone telling a mate that the day is nearly over.
explanation.walkthrough: Bruv is British street slang, short for brother, used as a term of address between friends.
explanation.definitionFit: Bruv is slang for a mate or pal, a casual way of addressing a male companion.

clue.text: A line observed in sport for Olympian

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: something observed in a place is seen within it, so it goes inside

parts.note: polo is a sport played on horseback
L is the abbreviation for line

explanation.surface: A line drawn on a sports field for an Olympic athlete.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Olympian' suggests an athlete, given the sport, but it means one of the gods of Mount Olympus.
explanation.definitionFit: Apollo is one of the twelve Greek gods who lived on Mount Olympus, so he is an Olympian deity.

clue.text: Good books devoured by stellar beast slowly

indicators.note: something devoured is eaten up and so ends up inside the eater

parts.note: Leo is the lion constellation
NT is the New Testament, part of the Good Book

explanation.surface: A star-sign beast slowly eating through some good books.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stellar beast' is the constellation Leo, the lion in the stars.
explanation.definitionFit: Lento is the Italian musical direction telling a performer to play at a slow tempo.

clue.text: Pace cut when reversing past split in road, always

indicators.note: going past something means coming after it, so this part follows the other

parts.note: a fork is where a road divides

indicators.note: a vehicle reversing travels backwards, so the letters run the other way
cutting something shortens it, so the word loses its final letter

parts.note: pace is speed

explanation.surface: A driver who slowed down while backing past a fork in the road.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pace cut' sounds like slowing down, but 'cut' means lose a letter. 'Reversing' fits the driving picture neatly while doing its wordplay job.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means permanently, for good, so it serves as an adverb meaning forever.

clue.text: Bump signalled after start of pregnancy

indicators.note: following something puts this part later in line, behind it
the start of a word is its beginning, so only the first letter is used

parts.note: the first letter of the word
rang a bell, as a signal

explanation.surface: A baby bump announced early in a pregnancy.
explanation.walkthrough: The baby-bump picture is the misdirection: a prang is British slang for a minor car crash.
explanation.definitionFit: A prang is a small collision, especially of a car, so it is a bump in the motoring sense.

clue.text: Reporter's narcissistic manner

indicators.note: a reporter delivers words by speaking, so it is the sound that counts

parts.note: a narcissist is vain

explanation.surface: A journalist with a self-absorbed style.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reporter' suggests a journalist, but it is anyone speaking the word.
explanation.definitionFit: Vein can mean a style or mood of speaking or writing, as in continuing in the same vein.

clue.text: Wetter South American native displayed clothes

indicators.note: as a verb, to clothe is to cover, so one part wraps around another

parts.note: displayed means showed
the rhea is a flightless bird of South America

explanation.surface: A rain-soaked South American local showing off their outfit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clothes' looks like a noun but is the verb, to dress. 'Wetter' looks like a comparative adjective; it is a thing that wets.
explanation.definitionFit: The fitting at the top of a shower sprays water over the bather, so it is literally something that wets.

clue.text: Long novel, questionable covers — one doesn't translate!

indicators.note: a covering goes all round, so one part sits wrapped inside the other

parts.note: a moot point is open to question

indicators.note: something novel is new, so these letters are made into a new arrangement

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A long novel with dubious covers that nobody will translate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Long novel' reads as a big book, but 'novel' is the signal to rearrange the word before it.
explanation.definitionFit: A monoglot speaks only a single language, so cannot render words from one tongue into another.

clue.text: Unfortunate twilight years, time after period in America?

indicators.note: following something places this part later, behind the other

parts.note: Americans call a full stop a period; it is a dot
an age is a long period of time

explanation.surface: Old age seen as an unlucky final chapter, spent in the United States.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Period' tempts as a span of time, given the years and time around it, but it is the American name for the punctuation mark.
explanation.definitionFit: Dotage is the feeble-minded state of old age, the unhappy later stage of life when faculties decline.
